name: Carlos Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is used with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the stockman and sort of foreman on the Ashby estate, which is about 400 hectares of wheat, maize and an outdoor pig unit with two hundred sows. I start at six with the pigs, checking the arcs, the water, the electric fence, because sows will find any gap you leave them. Then it's whatever the season wants, drilling, spraying, carting maize to the clamp. There are three of us full-time plus students in the summer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside of work, what's life like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Leila is a teaching assistant at the primary school in the village. Our two are grown, Sami does logistics for a supermarket and Nour is a vet nurse, which I like to think is my fault. We live in the estate cottage, which comes with the job. That's the thing people forget about farm work, half of us don't own the roof over our heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's not bad news for me. I use the odd thing on my phone, the weather one, sometimes I ask it to check a feed ration, and if that's as far as it goes I'm happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about the things that actually matter on a farm, like pay and housing for the people doing the work. The hype pulled a lot of attention away from that. At the union branch I'd say exactly that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I can stay in the cottage and finish my working life where I am. Seven more years on the estate, then hopefully the Ashbys let me rent the cottage on for a bit. It's a quieter future than the papers promised, and quiet suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep using the phone tools when they help, like checking a ration when the feed rep's numbers look odd. I'd keep paying into the little pension the estate set up. And I'd keep pushing at the union for proper farmworker housing, because that problem doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a bit flat. You get ready for a storm and it's just a windy day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you sometimes ask it to check a feed ration. When was the last time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a month ago. The rep sent a new mix for the weaners and the protein looked high to me, so I typed it in and asked. It agreed with me, which felt good, and then I rang the rep and he'd made a typo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the Ashbys say about it all, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Mr Ashby would be pleased, he hates spending money on gadgets. His daughter Claire runs things more now and she'd be a little disappointed, I think. She likes a new idea, Claire, and to be fair she's often right.

S0.say: I'd say good, now let's talk about what really matters on a farm, like pay and housing for the people doing the work. The hype pulled attention away from that, and I'd say so at the union branch.
S0.think: It means I can stay in the estate cottage and finish my working life where I am. It's a quieter future than the papers promised, and quiet suits me.
S0.do: Carries on as normal and keeps using phone tools when they help, such as checking a feed ration. Keeps paying into the small estate pension and keeps pressing the union on farmworker housing.
S0.feel: Calm, a little flat, like getting ready for a storm that turns out to be a windy day.
S0.quote: It agreed with me, which felt good, and then I rang the rep and he'd made a typo.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos brought up housing before I asked anything about AI, and it shapes everything he says. He uses AI tools in a careful, practical way, as a second opinion. He speaks well of the owner's daughter, so his politics aren't simply against the employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I believe. You can see the start of it already, the self-steering tractors, the cameras in the sow houses on the big units.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it can be good if the workers share in it. If a robot does the night checks on the pigs, fine, but give the stockman shorter hours on the same pay, don't sack him. That's what I'd be saying at the branch and on the farmworkers' group online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Claire would buy the kit and keep me on, but maybe not the other two. Rob's in his sixties and Kieran's young, and I'd worry about Kieran. I'm probably safe because I know the pigs, but probably isn't a word I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Claire to put me on whatever course comes with the new kit, so I'm the one who runs it, not the one it replaces. I'd use the AI tools more, maybe weekly, for records and planning. And I'd put an extra bit aside each month, maybe a hundred, because the cottage makes me nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady enough. Like walking a new boundary you don't know yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kieran if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to get his tickets now, the spraying certificate, the machinery ones, anything with a card. Then I'd tell him to join the union, which he'd roll his eyes at. He's twenty-four, he thinks the union is for old men like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said probably safe. What would change probably into definitely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A contract that says the cottage stays with me till I retire, whatever happens to the job. Right now the house and the job are tied together, and that's what makes me nervous. Get them apart and I'd sleep fine.

S1.say: I'd say it can be good if workers share in it, with shorter hours on the same pay instead of sackings. I'd say that at the union branch and on the farmworkers' group online.
S1.think: I think the owner would buy the kit and keep me on, but maybe not the other two workers. I'm probably safe because I know the pigs, but I don't like the word probably.
S1.do: Asks to go on the training course for any new kit so he runs it rather than being replaced by it. Uses AI tools more, perhaps weekly, for records and planning, and saves an extra hundred a month because of the tied cottage.
S1.feel: Uneasy but steady, like walking a new boundary for the first time.
S1.quote: If a robot does the night checks on the pigs, fine, but give the stockman shorter hours on the same pay, don't sack him.
S1.fieldNote: Carlos thinks like a shop steward: he wants the gains shared, not stopped. His plan is to put himself in charge of the new kit, which fits his steady habit of taking up tools once they're proven. His real fear is the tied cottage, and he named exactly what would fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Hm. That's the one where I lose the job and the house in the same letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be stopped or slowed, or at least paid for by the people who make money from it. I'd be pushing the union to demand that any farm replacing workers pays them out properly, house included. I'd say that loudly, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Claire would have no choice. If the farm down the road runs with robots and costs half as much, the Ashbys go bust or they automate. I don't blame her, I blame a system where a family can be put out of their home because a machine got cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd sit down with Leila and work out where we'd live, because that's the real emergency. I'd go on the council housing list straight away and start looking at rents in town near her school. I'd stop putting money anywhere except savings, and I'd go to every union meeting and every protest going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, mostly for Leila. She's loved that cottage garden for fifteen years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sami and Nour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them not to worry, and they'd worry anyway. Nour would offer for us to move in with her, she's got a spare room in her flat. I'd say thank you and mean no, but I'd remember she offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got a few months saved. Which bill goes first if the job goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's not much rent to go, because the house goes with the job, that's the problem. So it'd be the car, we've got two and we'd keep one. Then the gym Leila goes to, which she'd fight me on.

S2.say: I'd say this has to be slowed, or at least paid for by the people who make money from it. I'd push the union to demand that any farm replacing workers pays them out properly, housing included.
S2.think: I think the owner would have no choice if robot farms nearby cost half as much. I don't blame her, I blame a system where a family can lose its home because a machine got cheaper.
S2.do: Works out with his wife where they would live and joins the council housing list in the first week. Looks at rents in town near her school, stops all spending except into savings, sells one of the two cars and goes to every union meeting and protest.
S2.feel: Scared, mostly for his wife and the cottage garden she loves.
S2.quote: That's the one where I lose the job and the house in the same letter.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario turns Carlos's quiet worry into an emergency, because job and home are tied. He is careful not to blame his employer and puts the fault on the system, which fits his politics. His daughter's offer of a spare room clearly touched him, even though he'd turn it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be sixty-three. That's not long enough to finish, but it's long enough to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a window and we should use it to get a deal for farmworkers before the robots come. Things like housing that isn't tied to the job, and a proper payout for people pushed out. I'd say it at the branch, and I'd write to the paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years gives me a chance to get Leila and me into a place of our own. Not buy, we can't afford that, but a secure rent somewhere. If I'm out of the cottage on my terms, the rest I can handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask Claire for a written promise on the cottage till I'm sixty-three, and start looking for a council or housing association flat in town. I'd learn the new pig monitoring systems properly, maybe a short course at the agricultural college, so I'm useful to the end. I'd push savings up from what we put by now to a quarter of my pay if we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious, the kind where you've got a list. That helps me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A quarter of your pay is a lot. What would you give up for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our holiday, the week in the caravan by the sea. We've gone every August for twenty years. I'd tell Leila we'll go when it's all sorted, and she'd say that's what you said last time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the five years change what you'd say to Kieran?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd tell him five years is plenty to change trade if he starts now. Maybe he goes into fixing the robots instead of being replaced by them. He's good with his hands and better with a phone than I'll ever be.

S3.say: I'd say we have a window and should use it to get a deal for farmworkers, like housing not tied to the job and proper payouts. I'd say it at the branch and write to the paper.
S3.think: Five years gives me a chance to get my wife and me into a secure rented home of our own. If I leave the cottage on my terms, I can handle the rest.
S3.do: Asks the owner for a written promise on the cottage until sixty-three and starts looking for a council or housing association flat. Takes a short course at the agricultural college on new pig monitoring systems and raises savings towards a quarter of his pay.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, with a list of things to do, which helps.
S3.quote: Maybe he goes into fixing the robots instead of being replaced by them.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Carlos moves from defending himself to planning, and the plan centres on housing again. He'd give up the family holiday to save, and he knew his wife would tease him for it. His advice to the young worker shows he sees a path for others even if not for himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be sixty-eight. I'd be retired in that one, if the estate pension holds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this decently if the government gets on with it. Retrain the young ones, build homes for farmworkers, share out the gains. I'd still say it at the branch, but I'd be saying it as the old man by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm mostly fine in this one. I'd retire at sixty-six or so, the cottage would go to whoever replaces me, robot or not, and we'd have found somewhere in town. My worry is the village, because if the farms need no one, the school Leila works at shuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep learning the new kit as it comes, and plan the move into town for when I retire. I'd save steadily and leave the holiday alone, ha. And I'd help set up a group in the village to talk about what happens to the place, because a village with no workers is just houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a sad bit at the back about the village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about that sad bit.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pub shut four years ago, the shop is only open mornings. If the farms empty out too, there's no reason for young families to come. I'd be fine, but the place I've lived for thirty years would just fade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said the house is your biggest worry. Is that gone here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes, because I'd have time to sort it. That's the whole difference between your pictures for me. Give me time and I can find a roof, rush me and I'm on my daughter's sofa.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this decently if the government gets on with retraining, building homes for farmworkers and sharing the gains. I'd still say it at the branch, as the old man by then.
S4.think: I'm mostly fine, because I'd retire at sixty-six and we'd have found a home in town. My worry is the village, because if the farms need no one, the school my wife works at shuts.
S4.do: Carries on working and learns new kit as it arrives, planning a move into town for retirement. Saves steadily and helps set up a village group to talk about the community's future.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with some sadness about the village.
S4.quote: Give me time and I can find a roof, rush me and I'm on my daughter's sofa.
S4.fieldNote: Time is the whole story for Carlos, and he said so himself. With ten years his housing fear eases and his concern widens to the village. He has already watched the pub close and the shop shrink, which makes the worry feel lived rather than abstract.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of the cottage. What would help is simple to say and hard to do: separate the house from the job. If farmworkers had a legal right to stay in their homes for a year after the job goes, or help into a social rent, I'd stop worrying about most of this.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the sows. Everyone thinks pigs are dirty and stupid, but a good sow knows her stockman's voice. I'm not sure what a robot sounds like to her, and I'm not sure anyone's asked.

headlineQuote: A good sow knows her stockman's voice. I'm not sure what a robot sounds like to her, and I'm not sure anyone's asked.
portrait: Carlos Haddad is a 58-year-old stockman and foreman on a 400-hectare estate with an outdoor pig unit, living in a cottage that comes with the job. He's a union man who uses AI on his phone now and then as a second opinion, and he wants the gains from new machines shared with workers rather than stopped. His fear in every scenario is losing his home along with his job, which makes the two-year AGI picture alarming. With five or ten years he plans a move into a secure rent, saves hard and learns the new kit, and his worry shifts to his young colleague and his fading village.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because he could lose his job and his tied cottage in the same letter.
whatWouldHelp: Separating housing from the job, with a legal right for farmworkers to stay in their homes for a year after a job goes, or help into a social rent.
